Representative automotive part made with SMC 71 Business case The project demonstrated for the first time use of low cost textile grade carbon fiber SMC in conjunction with recycled carbon fibers. Traditional glass fiber SMC was also integrated in the study along with innovations in basalt SMC. Box sides, tailgate, cargo lid, headboard, in-bed trunk assemblies, multi piece SMC roof assemblies, trunk divider and trunk liners are a few example candidates where the project has immediate applications. The project provided new SMC intermediates such as recycled carbon fiber-glass fiber or TCF with glass fiber SMC, etc. with possibilities to provide many variations of these. These have strong commercial potential. Currently the cost of carbon-SMC commercially is ~$26/lb making it prohibitive except for high end performance applications. The current project provides avenues to create hybrid carbon-glass SMCs for much less. A detailed cost analysis would consider the volumes and procurement of the rCF and TCF and conversion to SMC. A ballpark cost basis is as follows. If we consider chopped TCF at $4.50/lb, rCF at $4/lb, SMC resin at $0.50/lb and the conversion cost at $1.50/lb, the hybrid SMC can be estimated at $11/lb. With higher volumes it is likely <$10/lb. This cost range makes the material attractive for automotive and industrial applications where carbon fiber SMC has had limitations thus far. Continuous progress on the line will enable further innovation and open the avenues for more materials – e.g.., epoxy, bismaleimides (aerospace applications), phenolics (battery applications), and thermoplastics (polypropylene, polyamides) for enhanced recyclability. Summary/Conclusions/Accomplishments This work resulted in various learnings and outcomes: The development of the multi-material SMC line progressed from SMC-V1 to SMC-V2. From the lessons learned in SMC-V1, the SMC-V2 incorporated servo motors over induction motors which gave the overall cutter system precision control and made it quiet. The addition of a 14-roll compaction unit at the end of the line in SMC-V2 enabled higher material wet out which was a limitation in the SMC-V1. The cutters were further updated to reduce the cantilever overhang of the fiber which enabled more uniform cut lengths for glass, carbon, and basalt fibers. The overall instrumentation and system control including a remote control operation was enabled in the SMC- V2. The line speed is capable of 10-20 ft/minute. The cutting modules were designed and engineered for cutting glass, basalt and textile grade carbon in 300k and 450-600k format widths. This does not exist anywhere commercially and was a key accomplishment. Uniform cut quality and fiber length were demonstrated for a range of fibers. The cutting trials were established for a range of fiber types. For all variants the fiber length had close to zero SD and hence perfect cuts.
